prompt:
A student uses a manual stopwatch to measure the time taken for a trolley to travel down an inclined runway.
(a) Identify one source of random error in this experiment. [1]
(b) Identify one source of systematic error that could affect the time measurements. [1]
(c) Describe how the student can modify the experimental procedure to minimize the effect of the random error identified in (a). [1]

mark_scheme.criterion: Part (a): Human reaction time variations when starting or stopping the stopwatch (or slight variations in trolley release position / air currents).
Part (b): Stopwatch running consistently fast or slow (calibration error), or an uncorrected zero offset, or runway friction causing a consistent deceleration not accounted for.
Part (c): Repeat the timing measurement multiple times under identical conditions and calculate the mean time (or use electronic light gates).

hints: For random error, think of things that change unpredictably from run to run.
For systematic error, think of an instrument fault that affects every run in the same direction.
How do we reduce unpredictable variations?
solution: (a) Human reaction time variations when starting and stopping the stopwatch. (b) A calibration error causing the stopwatch clock to run consistently too fast or too slow. (c) Repeat the descent several times and calculate the mean time.
teacher_walkthrough: (a) Random error: human reaction time varies unpredictably on each attempt.
(b) Systematic error: an internal timer calibration fault causes every second to be recorded as slightly longer or shorter than true time.
(c) Remedy: repeating the measurement several times and calculating the mean allows random variations to cancel partially.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored runway timing context distinguishing random reaction time from systematic calibration fault.
